description: We are a multi-disciplinary engineering and scientific team combining expertise in electrical, mechanical, and software engineering with agricultural science. Passionate about applied space technology, we bridge orbit and Earth. For NASA Space Apps Challenge , we are building TerraAdapt, a decision-support platform enabling farmers to optimize crop rotations and build climate-resilient fields.
summary:
AgroMind is a farm digital twin we built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, under the theme "Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data". It helps a farmer see how their fields are doing now and test how different crop rotations would cope with a changing climate. The demo farm is in Story County, Iowa.

The project has four modules. CropTwin holds the farm profile: field boundaries, soil, crop history and the farmer's priorities. CropDoctor compares each field's NASA MODIS greenness with that field's own 10-year normal(work in progress). When a field falls behind, it gives a cautious finding and a check to do in the field. The Simulator runs crop rotations over several seasons under NASA CMIP6 climate scenarios and reports the change compared with today's climate. Economics turns those weather years into money, using USDA and Iowa State figures or the farmer's own.

An assistant explains each page in plain language and quotes only that page's numbers. Every value is labelled as observed, modelled or scenario, with its source. The app works in English and Macedonian.
details:
A farmer starts in the farm profile. They draw each field on satellite imagery, then say what grows there, whether they irrigate, and how much they care about yield, saving water, avoiding bad years, soil health and margin. Soil values are prefilled from ISRIC SoilGrids.

Day to day they use the Command Center. It lists each field with its 30-day rainfall, average daily high and crop water demand, each next to the normal for that time of year, for today or for any date they pick. If a field drifts from its normal, the app says what it observed, how far off it is, one possible explanation, and what to go and check. AgroMind doesn't diagnose, because satellites and weather records can't rule out pests or disease.

Planning happens in the Simulator. It takes one field and up to four crop rotations, and replays each rotation over the 25 years of weather NASA POWER has for that spot (2001 to 2025). To look ahead, the farmer shifts that weather. They can set the shift by hand, say 2 °C hotter with 20% less rain, or load a NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 projection, which is the median of 6 climate models for SSP2-4.5 or SSP5-8.5 in the 2050s or 2080s. What comes back is a ranking by the farmer's priorities, with each rotation's change against today's climate.

Farm money puts a price on the same comparison. It works out the margin per hectare and for the whole field, today and in the scenario, from USDA price projections and Iowa State University cost budgets. A farmer who knows their own prices, costs and rent can type those in.

A farmer can also just ask. The assistant takes a sentence like "simulate 2 °C hotter with 20% less rain", opens the Simulator, sets the scenario and runs it while they watch. It lists every change it made, each one can be undone, and its answers come from numbers the app has already calculated.

The Simulator's physics is a set of published agronomic rules. It uses the FAO-56 crop water balance, published US crop responses to heat, and rotation effects, and we calibrated it against USDA county yields for Story County, Iowa, where our demo farm is. We chose rules over a trained model so that a farmer or an agronomist can check every step. The calibration only covers that one location, and the model is weak at telling one year from the next. So the app shows change against today's climate, and lists its assumptions and sources next to the results.

We want a farmer to be able to compare adaptation choices before planting and to see the evidence behind each number. After the hackathon we would like to take it beyond the demo farm and bring in more satellite data.

The front end is React and TypeScript with Vite, Tailwind, Leaflet, MapLibre and Recharts. The back end is Python with FastAPI and SQLite, and we test with Playwright. The interface is in English and Macedonian.
